prompt_text:
The figure gives an overview of the immune system and how nanoparticle-based CRISPR/Cas9 therapies may be delivered to immune cells in the body. The upper part summarizes immune-cell development from a hematopoietic stem cell into myeloid and lymphoid lineages, producing cells such as eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, neutrophils, dendritic cells, macrophages, natural killer cells, T cells, B cells, and plasma cells. Alongside this, a body diagram highlights major immune organs and tissues, including the thymus, lymph nodes, spleen, Peyer’s patches, skin, tonsils or mucous membranes, and bone marrow.

The lower part outlines the delivery pathway for nanoparticle CRISPR systems after local or systemic injection. The particles enter the blood, may be cleared by the liver or kidney, or reach target immune organs and then cells. Several barriers are emphasized: maintaining nanoparticle integrity in blood, crossing the vascular endothelium, avoiding off-target organs, achieving organ and cell specificity, diffusing through extracellular space, entering cells through the membrane, and finally reaching the nucleus. Overall, the figure conveys that successful immune-cell gene editing depends on navigating multiple biological obstacles from circulation to intracellular delivery.

entities.name: target immune organs and target immune cells
